name: Stedica CRM
author: Stedica

sections.description:
Stedica CRM keeps your contacts and companies inside your own WordPress site, in your own database, with no limit on records or users. There is no account to create, and the plugin contacts no other site unless you turn on something that needs one: External services below lists each.

Contacts and companies

  • Unlimited contacts, companies and users, custom fields of every common type, and tags, lists and lifecycle stages you can rename, reorder, add and remove.
  • Each email address belongs to one contact, and possible duplicates (same name or phone) can be merged, history and all, or marked as different people.
  • Data-quality checks flag invalid and throwaway emails, domains that take no mail, shared mailboxes, missing names and broken phone numbers.
  • Optional company logos from each company’s own website, and legal details from Companies House, GLEIF, SEC EDGAR and the French company directory.
  • If two people edit a record at once, nobody’s changes are lost.

Deals and pipelines

  • Unlimited pipelines with their own stages and win probabilities, on a drag-and-drop board or a list.
  • Several contacts per deal, line items, won and lost reasons, a weighted forecast, and deals that went quiet.

Quotes, invoices and the client portal

  • Turn a deal into a quote in one click, with taxes per line, discounts, terms and your logo. Clients get a print-ready page and accept by typing their name or decline with a reason.
  • An accepted quote becomes an invoice in one click. Numbers use your prefixes and never repeat; record payments by transfer, card, cash or check. With WooCommerce, clients can pay through your checkout.
  • A client portal block where contacts you invite see their quotes and invoices, download shared files, update their details and email choices, and request their data or its deletion.

Timeline, tasks and reports

  • A timeline of notes, calls, meetings, emails and changes for each contact and company, tasks with due dates and owners, and a Today screen.
  • Connect a shared mailbox over IMAP and emails from or to your contacts land on their timeline. Other mail is ignored, and the mailbox is never changed.
  • Reports on pipeline, team activity, lead sources, email, automations, store revenue, quotes and invoices, and data quality, each downloadable as CSV.

Segments, import and export

  • Filter contacts by any field, tag, list, task or company detail and save it as a segment that stays up to date. Tag, list, assign or delete in bulk.
  • Import a CSV with columns matched for you, or move from FluentCRM, Jetpack CRM, WP ERP, WP-CRM System, Groundhogg, MailPoet, FunnelKit Automations, HubSpot, Mailchimp or your site’s users. Consent is never invented.
  • Someone who unsubscribed from a list is never put back on it by an import, a bulk action or a merge.
  • Export any list or segment to CSV, with sensitive fields left out unless an administrator asks for them.

Lead scoring that explains itself

  • Fit (A to D) and Engagement (1 to 4) combine into a grade from A1 to D4. Fit rules are filters; engagement rules give capped points for visits, forms, email clicks, calls, meetings and deals, fading over a half-life you choose.
  • “Why this score?” lists every rule and point, and you can preview how many contacts a change would move. Templates for six kinds of business and a report on how each grade converts.
  • Contacts who object to profiling are not scored, and sensitive fields never feed a rule. Scores decide whom to follow up first, never decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

Email campaigns

  • Newsletters to lists and segments, now or later, written in the block editor with merge tags, a phone preview and a test send.
  • Only people who consented or subscribed receive them; anyone who unsubscribed, bounced or complained is left out, checked again before each email.
  • Unsubscribe links, one-click unsubscribe and your postal address in every campaign; subject A/B tests, per-link reports and a send log.
  • Send through WordPress’s own mail (any SMTP plugin works), Amazon SES, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, Brevo or Resend; Site Health checks your SPF, DMARC and DKIM.

Automations

  • Build a flow from a trigger and steps, or start from one of twelve recipes.
  • Triggers: contacts, deals, quotes, invoices, forms, emails, WooCommerce orders and carts, accounts, website visits, dates, segments, webhooks, or by hand.
  • Steps send emails, update the contact, create tasks, deals and notes, notify your team, send webhooks and start other automations, with waits, if/else branches and goals. Automation emails follow the campaign consent rules.

WooCommerce and Easy Digital Downloads

  • Every order adds or updates the buyer’s contact with their orders, lifetime value (less refunds) and RFM segment. Past orders import in the background, and paid orders can become won deals.
  • Abandoned carts are saved once a shopper types their email at checkout; shoppers in the EU, the UK and unknown countries tick a box first. Up to three optional recovery emails link back to the filled cart.
  • Block and classic checkouts, either order storage, and Easy Digital Downloads orders.

The plugins you already use

  • Courses from Tutor LMS, LifterLMS, LearnDash and Stedica LMS; memberships and subscriptions from MemberPress, Paid Memberships Pro, Kadence Memberships (Restrict Content Pro), WooCommerce Memberships and WooCommerce Subscriptions; bookings from LatePoint and Amelia; tickets from Fluent Support and SupportCandy; answers from Stedica Surveys.
  • Their events reach the contact’s timeline, automations and lead scoring. Each is off until you turn it on.

AI assistants and the command line

  • WordPress Abilities let AI assistants and MCP tools search contacts, log calls, add tasks, move deals and explain scores, with the signed-in user’s permissions. Each is off until you turn it on.
  • AI assist, off until you turn it on, summarises a contact, company or deal and drafts emails through the AI service connected to WordPress 7.0 or later. Email addresses, phone numbers and custom fields are never sent.
  • wp stedica-crm commands to import, export, recount, rescore, purge and send a test email.

Forms, consent and website activity

  • A form block or shortcode (inline, pop-up or slide-in) with spam filtering and no captcha, or your forms in WPForms, Gravity Forms, Fluent Forms, Contact Form 7, Formidable Forms, Ninja Forms, Elementor Pro or Stedica Surveys. List sign-ups confirm by email first.
  • A Restricted content block shows a lead magnet once the visitor sends a form that adds the right tag.
  • Every consent, withdrawal and objection is kept, never edited, with the exact wording shown.
  • Website activity, off until you turn it on: the pages a contact visited, their searches and where they first came from, with the consent rules in the FAQ.

Mobile app

  • Add your site’s /crm/ address to a phone’s home screen for a full-screen app made for one hand; the same app runs inside wp-admin.
  • An optional offline copy on each device; changes made offline are sent once back online.
  • Task reminders as notifications on phones and computers, once an administrator turns push reminders on.
  • A Manual button beside every page title, and a dashboard widget.

Roles, privacy and languages

  • Five roles: CRM Admin, CRM Manager, CRM Sales, CRM Marketing and CRM Viewer. Optionally, sales users see only their own and unassigned records, enforced on the server for every request.
  • An activity log, personal-data export and erasure, retention limits and suggested privacy-policy text. See the FAQ.
  • Each user sees the CRM in their own language. Translations come from translate.wordpress.org, where you can help translate Stedica CRM.

External services

The plugin uses an outside service only when you choose one: an email provider, a mailbox, an automation webhook, an import from HubSpot or Mailchimp, AI assist, push reminders, company logos, a company registry or a Premium licence.

Email. Until an administrator picks a provider in Stedica CRM → Settings → Email, all email goes through WordPress’s own wp_mail(). The chosen service is called only to send the plugin’s emails (campaigns, automation emails, team notices, tests, recovery and confirmation emails, quotes, invoices and one-to-one emails). Each email gives it the recipient’s and sender’s addresses and names, the reply-to address, subject, HTML and text body, unsubscribe headers and a send number, which it returns with bounce and complaint reports.

  • Amazon SES: email.<region>.amazonaws.com, plus Amazon SNS certificates from sns.<region>.amazonaws.com to verify bounce reports. AWS Customer Agreement, Privacy Notice.
  • Postmark: api.postmarkapp.com. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.
  • SendGrid: api.sendgrid.com. Terms of Service, Privacy Notice.
  • Mailgun: api.mailgun.net or api.eu.mailgun.net. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.
  • Brevo: api.brevo.com. Terms of Use, Privacy Policy.
  • Resend: api.resend.com. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.

Site Health’s SPF, DMARC and DKIM checks use your server’s own DNS lookups.

Mailboxes. Until an administrator connects one in Stedica CRM → Settings → Mailboxes, no mail is read. Then, every five minutes and on Check now or Test connection, the plugin signs in to the IMAP server entered, over SSL/TLS or STARTTLS, with its user name and password (stored encrypted), opens the chosen folders read-only and reads what arrived since the last check. It never marks, moves or deletes a message, and keeps only emails from or to your contacts. The server belongs to your mail provider (such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or your host), whose terms and privacy policy apply.

Automation webhooks. A “Send a webhook” step posts JSON to the https address entered in it, when a contact reaches the step: the contact’s ID, email, first and last name, phone, job title, lifecycle stage, grade, tags and lists; the automation’s ID, name and trigger; your site’s address; and a delivery number and time. The address belongs to a service you chose, whose terms and privacy policy apply.

Imports. Stedica CRM → Import contacts reads from HubSpot or Mailchimp only while someone previews or runs an import with a key they enter. The key is sent with each request and never saved. Nothing about your site’s contacts is sent: only the key, the fields to read, record ids and page markers, and your site’s address in the user agent.

  • HubSpot: api.hubapi.com, with a private app access token; reads contacts, companies and notes. Customer Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.
  • Mailchimp: <dc>.api.mailchimp.com, the data center at the end of the API key (such as us21); reads audiences, fields and members. Standard Terms of Use, Privacy Statement.

AI assist. Off until an administrator turns it on in Stedica CRM → Settings → Integrations. It uses the AI client built into WordPress 7.0 and later, so requests go to the AI provider connected to your site, under that provider’s terms and privacy policy. A request goes out only when a user clicks Summarise on a contact, company or deal, or Draft with AI in the email form. It contains the record’s name, job title, company, lifecycle stage, grade, tags, deal or order figures and up to 30 recent timeline entries (type, date and subject); a draft adds what the user typed and their name. Email addresses, phone numbers and custom fields are never sent.

Push reminders. Off until an administrator turns them on in Stedica CRM → Settings → General; then each person chooses per device. Their browser gives the plugin an address at its push service, kept only if it belongs to a service below. When a task falls due (or 15 or 60 minutes before), the plugin posts the task’s title, a short heading and a link to the app to that address, encrypted end to end so the push service cannot read it, with a signed token naming your site’s address. Test notifications work the same way.

  • Google (Chrome and other Chromium browsers): fcm.googleapis.com. Firebase Terms, Privacy Policy.
  • Mozilla (Firefox): *.push.services.mozilla.com. Terms of Service, Firefox Privacy Notice.
  • Apple (Safari and Home Screen apps on iPhone and iPad): web.push.apple.com and *.push.apple.com. Legal, Privacy Policy.
  • Microsoft (Edge): *.notify.windows.com. Services Agreement, Privacy Statement.

Company logos. Off until an administrator turns them on in Stedica CRM → Settings → Company data. The plugin asks each company’s own website for its home page and the icon it names, or /favicon.ico, every 30 days and when the website changes, sending only what WordPress sends with any request (including your site’s address in the user agent). The company’s own terms apply. Turning logos off deletes them.

Company registries. Used to look up a company’s legal name, registration number, status and registered address. Each is off until an administrator turns it on in Stedica CRM → Settings → Company data, and is called only when someone searches, picks a result or clicks Refresh on a company. The request carries what they typed or the number picked, and nothing about your contacts.

  • Companies House (UK company register, run by the UK government): searches and company details from api.company-information.service.gov.uk, sent with the administrator’s free API key (stored encrypted). Terms of use: GOV.UK terms and conditions and the API developer guidelines. Privacy policy: Companies House personal information charter.
  • GLEIF (Legal Entity Identifiers): searches and records from api.gleif.org. Terms of use: LEI Data Terms of Use. Privacy policy: GLEIF Privacy Policy.
  • SEC EDGAR (US public companies, run by the US Securities and Exchange Commission): the list of company names from www.sec.gov (kept for a day) and company details from data.sec.gov. The SEC asks automated clients to identify themselves, so requests carry your site’s name and admin email address in the user agent. Terms of use: Accessing EDGAR Data. Privacy policy: SEC Privacy Information.
  • Annuaire des entreprises (French company directory, SIRENE, run by the French government’s digital agency DINUM): searches and company details from recherche-entreprises.api.gouv.fr. Terms of use: API Recherche d’entreprises access conditions and data.gouv.fr terms of use. Privacy policy: Annuaire des entreprises privacy policy.

Mail-domain check. On by default (turn it off in Stedica CRM → Settings → Company data): your server’s own DNS resolver is asked whether each contact’s email domain has a mail server. Common free providers are skipped, answers are kept 30 days, and nothing is sent to the address.

Freemius, for the optional Stedica CRM Premium. The bundled Freemius SDK sends nothing unless an administrator opts in, starts the trial or activates a licence. Then api.freemius.com receives the site’s address, that user’s name and email, and the WordPress, PHP and plugin versions; no CRM data. An upgrade link opens Freemius’s checkout at checkout.freemius.com in the browser; the plugin itself sends nothing to it. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy. The SDK is GPL-3.0.
sections.installation:
1. Install and activate the plugin.
  2. Open Stedica CRM in the WordPress admin menu.
  3. On your phone, open Stedica CRM → Mobile app (your site’s /crm/ address), sign in, and add it to the home screen.
sections.faq:
Where is my data stored?

In your WordPress database, in tables that start with your table prefix followed by stedica_crm_. Nothing is sent anywhere else.

Files you share through the client portal, and CSV files while they are imported, are kept in a folder with a random name inside your uploads folder, under random file names. The folder has rules that block direct access on Apache and IIS; on nginx, which does not read them, the random names keep the files from being found. Clients download shared files through a checked link that only works for them and your team.

Company logos, when you turn them on, are kept in a stedica-crm-logos folder in your uploads folder, under names that cannot be guessed. Someone who turns on the offline copy under This device in the app keeps what they open in that browser, and changes made offline until they are sent; the copy is removed when they turn it off or log out, or after 7 days.

Does the plugin connect to external services?

Only if you choose to. By default email goes through WordPress’s own mail function, and the plugin makes no requests to any outside service. If you connect Amazon SES, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, Brevo or Resend, each email is sent through that service. If an automation has a “Send a webhook” step, it posts to the address you entered. If you move your contacts in from HubSpot or Mailchimp, the importer reads them from that service with the key you give it. If you turn on AI assist, a record’s details go to the AI service connected to WordPress when someone asks for a summary or a draft. If you connect a mailbox, the plugin signs in to that mail server to read new mail. If you turn on push reminders, encrypted reminders go through the push service of each browser that asked for them. If you turn on company logos, each company’s own website is asked for its icon. If you turn on a company registry, what someone searches for goes to that registry. See “External services” below. The check that an email domain takes mail uses your server’s own DNS. Visitor countries come only from what your server already knows (headers set by your host or CDN, or WooCommerce’s geolocation database on your server); IP addresses are never sent to a lookup service.

Does the plugin track anyone or send data to Stedica?

No data goes to Stedica, and there is no usage tracking or “phone home”. Every way of following what people do is off until an administrator turns it on, and what it records stays in your own database: website activity (which also waits for each visitor’s consent in your cookie banner, as described below), click tracking in emails and open tracking in emails. The optional Freemius SDK, for Stedica CRM Premium, sends nothing unless an administrator opts in, starts the trial or activates a licence (see “External services”).

Which cookies does it set?

None until something below applies. scrm_vid (13 months) recognises a returning visitor, and is set only when website activity is on and the visitor may be tracked. scrm_optout (13 months) remembers that a visitor asked not to be tracked. scrm_unlock (6 months) is set only when a visitor sends a form to read restricted content, so that content stays open for them. scrm_cart_optout (1 year) remembers that a shopper asked not to have their cart saved; saved carts otherwise rely on WooCommerce’s own session cookie. The plugin describes them to cookie banners that support the WP Consent API.

How does website activity respect consent?

It is off until you turn it on, and even then nobody is tracked until they consent: with a cookie banner that supports the WP Consent API, the banner’s “statistics” choice decides, for every visitor wherever they are. Without such a banner, nobody is tracked. Global Privacy Control is always respected. No IP addresses are stored with visits, which are kept 90 days for unknown visitors and 13 months for contacts (both adjustable).

Consent records cover email marketing, text messages, profiling and scoring, data enrichment, and sharing with ad platforms, with the purpose, time, source, exact wording and the address each came from. An objection stops all of them.

How is a score worked out, and can I see why?

Fit is the sum of the points of the fit rules a contact matches, from 0 to 100. Engagement is the sum of the points their recent activity earned, each halving after the half-life you set, also from 0 to 100. Open a contact and choose “Why this score?” to see every rule and every point. The same explanation is part of the personal-data export.

Can I put something secret in a Restricted content block?

The block keeps its content out of the page until the visitor qualifies, but WordPress’s own site search still searches the text inside it. Use it for lead magnets, not for secrets: for a download or a coupon code, put the file or code somewhere protected and link to it from inside the block.

What does the plugin do to help with privacy?

An activity log records who created, changed, imported, exported, merged or deleted records. It stores field names, never the values, so it never keeps personal data that you later erase.

The plugin works with WordPress’s own personal data export and erasure tools, and suggests text for your privacy policy.

Saved carts are deleted 90 days after their last change (you choose, from 30 to 365 days).

A contact’s emails, clicks and unsubscribes are part of their personal-data export, and erasing the contact deletes them; campaign totals stay. Emails logged from a connected mailbox are timeline entries, so the same applies to them. So is what each automation did for them, which erasing deletes too, and so are the courses, memberships, bookings, tickets and surveys that integrations you turned on added to their timeline.

Quotes, invoices and the files shared with a contact are part of their export. Erasing deletes their quotes, draft invoices and shared files, and removes their client portal access; issued invoices are legal records, so they stay with the billing details printed on them, and the eraser says so. In the client portal, clients can ask for their export or erasure themselves; the request goes through WordPress’s own confirmation email and waits for you in Tools.

Uninstalling keeps your data unless you turn on “Delete all CRM data when the plugin is deleted”.

These are tools to help you meet your privacy obligations. Using them does not by itself make a site compliant with any law.

What happens when I deactivate or delete the plugin?

Deactivating keeps everything. Deleting keeps your contacts too, unless an administrator turned on “Delete all CRM data when the plugin is deleted” in the CRM settings.

Can other plugins extend it?

Yes. The REST API lives under stedica-crm/v1. Records fire actions when they are created, updated and deleted (for example stedica_crm_contact_created), other plugins can add screens to the app, and the stedica_crm_integrations filter adds an integration with another plugin.

Where is the source of the app’s JavaScript?

In the plugin’s src folder. The files in build are compiled from it with npm install --legacy-peer-deps and npm run build, using the package.json and webpack.config.js that come with the plugin.
sections.changelog:
1.16.0

  • Contacts: buttons above the list filter by lifecycle stage and show how many contacts are in each.
  • Deals: open pipeline, weighted forecast, open deals and average deal as figures above the board.
  • Companies: each company shows its number of contacts, linked to them, and its open deals.
  • Tasks: each tab shows how many tasks it holds, and Today switches to Overdue when only overdue tasks are left.
  • Reports: icons on the figures and a short introduction on each tab.
  • Quotes and invoices: figures for the last 90 days (quoted, accepted, still owed, overdue) and state filters with counts.
  • Email: sending figures for the last 90 days and campaign status filters with counts.
  • Automations: status filters with counts, and ready-made recipes to start from.
  • Store: customer and abandoned cart figures with icons.
  • Forms: figures for forms on, entries and the latest entry, and a find box for long lists.
  • Activity log: filter by kind of record, with counts.
  • Settings: a side menu grouped by topic, with a short description of each section.
  • Long amounts in figures stay on one line.

1.15.1

  • Fix: the mobile app no longer shows “This screen ran into a problem” on sites where an optimisation plugin, such as SiteGround Optimizer, serves a minified copy of its script.
  • If a screen cannot load after an update, the page reloads once, then explains what happened with buttons to reload or go back to Today.
  • The menu is grouped into Sales, Marketing, Insights, Connect and Admin, and each screen has a short description under its title.

1.15.0

  • A new Today home page: the day and what is due at a glance, buttons to add a contact, deal, task or company, key figures, and your tasks and deals beside the pipeline by stage and the newest contacts.
  • The CRM screens in the WordPress admin use the full width of the page, and settings show their fields in two columns on wide screens.

1.14.0

  • With Stedica Surveys & Forms active, the Stedica CRM form block links to it for longer forms with steps, file uploads, calculations or payments.

1.13.0

  • Forms built in Stedica Surveys (5.47.0 or later) connect like any other form plugin, and from Stedica Surveys itself. Fields are matched to contact fields from what they hold (email, first and last name, phone, company, job title), and the email consent box sets the form’s consent.
  • A form sent from Stedica Surveys puts its answers on the contact’s timeline, with a link to the entry.
  • Survey answers from a connected Stedica Surveys form are not recorded twice.
  • Developers can add form plugins through the stedica_crm_capture_providers filter, and stedica_crm_form_submitted now passes what came with the submission.

1.12.2

  • Website activity now waits for every visitor’s consent, wherever they are. With a cookie banner that supports the WP Consent API, its “statistics” choice decides; without one, nobody is tracked. The setting to track UK visitors without asking is gone.
  • Developers can connect other consent tools through the stedica_crm_tracking_consent filter.

1.12.1

  • Click tracking in emails is now off until you turn it on, like open tracking and website activity.
  • The forms on the unsubscribe, email preferences, sign-up confirmation and quote pages now carry a security check (nonce) as well as their signed link.
  • Quote, invoice and email pages load their styles and print button as registered files instead of inline code.
  • Translations are delivered by translate.wordpress.org instead of being bundled in the plugin.
  • The External services section names each company registry’s terms of use and privacy policy.

1.12.0

  • Stedica Surveys: the contact form a survey shows before its questions or its result can be connected under Forms, like any other form plugin, with field mapping, tags, a list and consent.
  • Stedica Surveys: an answered survey now reaches the contact through its lead form, so visitors who are not signed in and answer no email question are recorded too. The timeline shows the result.
  • Fixed: a signed-in staff member trying out a survey with a visitor’s details no longer gets that visitor’s survey on their own record.

1.11.2

  • Accessibility: an empty Deals board and the line items table can be scrolled by keyboard, and the Edit, Delete and Show more links on the timeline are easier to tap.
  • Accessibility: the phone layout of the Activity log and the Quotes and invoices list now gives screen readers a correct structure.

1.11.1

  • Fixed: the commands in this readme that rebuild the app from its source failed on a clean install.
  • Fixed: the do-not-email Reason filter listed a reason this plugin never sets.
  • Corrected the help text on the automation Goal step and on sensitive custom fields, which did not say what actually happens.
  • Extensions can add do-not-email reasons, and can ask whether an AI service is connected.

1.11.0

  • New: a setup checklist. A short notice on the Plugins page and a card on Today lead to a Setup page with the steps for a new site. Steps tick themselves as you finish them, you can do them in any order, and you can skip what you do not need. Nothing in the CRM waits for it.
  • Sites that already have contacts start with the card hidden. The list is still in Settings, on the General tab.
  • The Manual on every page was checked against the plugin and brought up to date.
  • Extensions can add steps to the checklist and sections to a page’s Manual.

1.10.1

  • Maintenance release. Nothing changes in how the plugin works.

1.10.0

  • Fixed: a goal step could pull a contact out of a different path or branch of an automation. A goal now only moves a contact forward along their own path.
  • Automations can have steps with named paths, an “otherwise” path, and sections in their reports, for extensions to use. The run log, totals, export, import and copies handle them.
  • Extensions can show values in the campaigns list, and use AI assist’s connection and list of allowed facts. Stedica CRM Premium uses these.

1.9.0

  • Extensions can show columns in the contacts list, as they already could in the companies list. Stedica CRM Premium’s predictive score uses this.

1.8.0

  • Numbered with Stedica CRM Premium 1.8.0. No changes to the free plugin.

1.7.0

  • Extensions can add values to contacts and companies, add list parameters and filters, show columns in the companies list and reuse the scoring rule editor. This is what Stedica CRM Premium’s scoring models and account scores build on.
  • The do-not-email list has a new reason, “failed a check”, for addresses an email check found invalid. Marketing obeys it like the other reasons.
  • Imports announce each contact they create, so an extension can act on it.

1.6.0

  • Bundles the Freemius SDK for the optional Stedica CRM Premium. It stays silent until an administrator opts in, starts a trial or activates a licence, and nothing in the free plugin depends on it.
  • Fixed: an email logged from a shared mailbox could lose its last characters, or show its accented letters wrongly, when it was sent in base64 with no final line break.

1.5.1

  • Fixed: reactivating the plugin on a site with WooCommerce no longer logs a “translation loading triggered too early” notice. The daily tracking job is now scheduled once WordPress has loaded translations.

1.5.0

  • Mailboxes: connect shared mailboxes over IMAP and every email from or to one of your contacts is logged on their timeline, with replies linked to the email they answer and attachments listed. Mail from anyone else is ignored, nobody is added as a contact, and the mailbox is never changed.
  • The app works offline on each device that turns it on: what you opened stays readable, and notes, tasks and contact changes are kept and sent when you are back online.
  • Task reminders as push notifications on phones and computers, at the due time or 15 or 60 minutes before. Off until an administrator turns them on; each person chooses per device.
  • Company logos from each company’s own website, off until you turn them on.
  • Look a company up in Companies House, GLEIF, SEC EDGAR or the French company directory and keep its legal name, number, status and registered address. Each registry is off until you turn it on.
  • Data-quality checks on every contact: invalid and throwaway emails, domains that take no mail, shared mailboxes, missing names, names in all capitals or lower case, phone numbers that are not numbers and contacts with no way to reach them. A filter, a chip on the contact and a Data quality report.
  • Possible duplicates: contacts with the same name or phone number, listed to merge or mark as different people, and noted on the contact’s page.
  • Rename a saved segment, change its filter or delete it from the Contacts screen.
  • Manuals for the new screens, in English and Spanish.

1.4.0

  • Integrations with the plugins you already use, each off until you turn it on: Easy Digital Downloads; Tutor LMS, LifterLMS, LearnDash and Stedica LMS; MemberPress, Paid Memberships Pro, Kadence Memberships (Restrict Content Pro), WooCommerce Memberships and WooCommerce Subscriptions; LatePoint and Amelia; Fluent Support and SupportCandy; and Stedica Surveys.
  • Their events reach the person’s contact on the timeline, start automations (new trigger groups for courses, memberships, subscriptions, bookings, support and surveys) and earn lead-scoring points.
  • Easy Digital Downloads orders count like WooCommerce’s: lifetime value, RFM segments, the Store screen and report, won deals, and a background import of past orders.
  • Nine abilities for the WordPress Abilities API, so AI assistants and MCP tools can work with the CRM as the signed-in user. Each one is off until you turn it on.
  • AI assist, off until you turn it on: summaries of contacts, companies and deals, and email drafts, through the AI service connected to WordPress 7.0 or later.
  • wp stedica-crm commands: import, export, recount, rescore, purge and send-test.
  • A Mailchimp unsubscribe now takes the person off that audience’s list only, instead of withdrawing their email consent everywhere.

1.3.0

  • Quotes and invoices: from a deal’s line items or from scratch, with taxes, discounts, notes, terms and your business details and logo. Send them by email or link; clients print them or save them as a PDF, and accept or decline quotes online.
  • Accepted quotes become invoices in one click. Invoices get their number when issued, take payments, and can be voided; numbers never repeat.
  • With WooCommerce, clients can pay invoices online through your shop’s checkout.
  • Six automation triggers: quote sent, accepted and declined, and invoice issued, paid and overdue.
  • A client portal block: clients sign in to see their quotes and invoices, download files you share, correct their details, choose their emails and ask for their data or its deletion.
  • Give or remove portal access and share files from the contact’s page, with the date each file was first downloaded.
  • Reports in tabs: Pipeline, Activity (calls, meetings, notes, emails and tasks done, by person and over time), Sources (new contacts and won deals by first source, UTM campaign and first form), Email (sent, delivered, opened, clicked, unsubscribed, bounced and marked as spam, over time and by email), Automations (started, finished, stopped and failed), Store (revenue, orders and customers by RFM segment and by saved segment) and Quotes and invoices. Every tab has a period picker and a CSV download.
  • Sales users who see only their own records see only those records’ figures in every report.
  • Quotes, invoices and shared files are part of the personal-data export; erasing keeps only issued invoices, which are legal records.
  • Manuals for quotes, invoices and the client portal, in English and Spanish.

1.2.0

  • Automations: a flow builder with triggers for contacts, scoring, deals, forms, email, WooCommerce orders and carts, WordPress accounts, website visits, dates, segments, webhooks and adding people by hand.
  • Steps that send emails, tag, change lists, fields, stage and owner, create tasks, deals and notes, notify your team, send webhooks and start or stop other automations; waits, if/else branches and goals.
  • Twelve recipes with their emails written, from a welcome series to win-back after 90 days.
  • Move from FluentCRM, Jetpack CRM, WP ERP, WP-CRM System, Groundhogg, MailPoet, FunnelKit Automations, HubSpot, Mailchimp or the site’s WordPress users, with companies, tags, lists and each member’s status, custom fields and notes. Consent is never invented, and running a move again adds nothing twice.
  • Automation emails follow the same consent rules as campaigns and are checked again just before they go.
  • Each contact’s path through an automation, step by step, on the automation and on the contact’s page. Add people by hand, or many at once from the contact list.
  • Versions, pause, copy, and export and import of automations between sites.
  • New segment filter: in, not in, started or finished an automation. Automation events on the contact timeline and in the activity log.
  • A new capability, stedica_crm_manage_automations, for CRM Admins, CRM Managers, CRM Marketing and site administrators.
  • Manuals for the Automations screens, in English and Spanish.

1.1.0

  • Email campaigns: lists and segments, the block editor with your design, merge tags, templates, a test send, scheduling, pause and cancel, a second subject for half the audience, and a report with clicks per link and every recipient.
  • Campaigns go only to people who consented to email or subscribed to a list, with an unsubscribe link, your postal address and a one-click unsubscribe header. A page where people can leave a list, choose their lists or stop all marketing email.
  • Send through WordPress’s own mail or straight through Amazon SES, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, Brevo or Resend, with bounces and complaints coming back to a do-not-email list.
  • A send log that says why an email did not go, and Site Health checks for SPF, DMARC, the postal address and scheduled jobs.
  • Double opt-in for form sign-ups to a list, on by default.
  • Abandoned-cart recovery emails: up to three, with the cart’s contents and a link that refills the cart.
  • Email a contact from their page. A contact’s page shows the emails they received and clicked.
  • New segment filters for campaigns received, opened and clicked, recent clicks and the do-not-email list. Scoring templates give points for email clicks.
  • The dashboard widget shows the last campaign and warns about email problems.
  • A new capability, stedica_crm_send_email, for CRM Admins, CRM Managers, CRM Marketing and site administrators. Email settings and keys need the settings capability.
  • Manuals for the Email screens, in English and Spanish.

1.0.0

  • First stable release, after a security review, an accessibility audit and a load test with 100,000 contacts.
  • Fields marked sensitive stay out of contact and deal lists and filters for everyone but CRM administrators.
  • “Own records only” now also limits filters, segments, and tag and list counts.
  • Restricted content opens only for visitors who qualify, and only on posts whose author can use the CRM.
  • Forms, website activity and saved carts are rate limited, with an IPv6 network counted as one visitor. Form redirects go only to web addresses.
  • Site accounts are linked to their contacts only when that is proven: at registration, through the account’s own form or order, or once on upgrade by matching email.
  • A withdrawn consent or an objection is never granted again by a later form or import. Adding contacts to a list in bulk asks you to confirm consent.
  • Form entries that reached no contact are deleted after 90 days. The personal-data export pages through long timelines.
  • The app cannot be shown inside another site’s frame.
  • Faster product filters, deal attention panel and calibration report on large sites.
  • Better colour contrast, page landmarks, and focus that stays on a deal after you move it on the board.
  • The contact list fits laptop screens, with two tags per row and a count for the rest.
  • The menu is now Stedica CRM, with the Stedica icon in colour. The icon also leads every page title, and Today in the WordPress admin opens with the Stedica banner.
  • A Manual button beside every page title, with a guide to that page.
  • Spanish (Spain) translation, beside Spanish (Mexico). Every screen loads its translations from translate.wordpress.org language packs too, and dates, “3 hours ago” and numbers follow each user’s language.
  • On WooCommerce sites, people with a CRM role can open the CRM in the WordPress admin and keep the toolbar. WooCommerce had sent them to My account.
  • A Stedica CRM widget on the WordPress dashboard: contacts, new contacts, open deals and pipeline, with warnings for overdue tasks, deals that need attention, failed form submissions and imports, and scheduled jobs that are behind.

0.6.0

  • WooCommerce sync: every order adds or updates the buyer’s contact, with orders, lifetime value, average order, and refunds and cancellations on the timeline. Past orders import in the background.
  • RFM scores and eleven segments, with a heatmap and segment list on the new Store screen.
  • Optional won deals for paid orders, and buyers moved to the Customer stage.
  • Abandoned-cart capture at checkout, with consent by region and Global Privacy Control, abandoned and recovered carts on the timeline, and cart figures on the Store screen.
  • An Orders card on the contact page; Lifetime value, Orders, Last order and RFM segment columns; segments by purchases and RFM; engagement points for orders and abandoned carts.
  • Orders and saved carts in the personal-data export and erasure.

0.5.0

  • Lead scoring: fit and engagement models, the A1–D4 grade matrix, negative rules, limits per period and decay.
  • Receipts and “Why this score?” on every contact; scores in the personal-data export.
  • A simulator that shows the impact of rule changes before you save them.
  • Thresholds that move the lifecycle stage and show newly qualified leads on Today, with optional owner emails.
  • Six scoring templates and a calibration report.
  • Email type (business, free, shared, disposable) on every contact; segments by grade, fit, engagement and email type; a Grade column in the contact list.

0.4.0

  • Form block and shortcode, shown in the page, in a pop-up or sliding in, with spam filtering that needs no captcha.
  • Connections for WPForms, Gravity Forms, Fluent Forms, Contact Form 7, Formidable Forms, Ninja Forms and Elementor Pro forms, with suggested field mapping.
  • Consent records with the exact wording, objections that stop every purpose, Global Privacy Control, and consent recorded for imports.
  • Website activity, off by default: page views, site searches, first and latest source, page groups and “last seen”, following the WP Consent API or the visitor’s region.
  • Restricted content block for lead magnets.
  • Segments by consent, page group, site search, source and last visit. Source and Last seen columns in the contact list.

0.3.0

  • Deals and unlimited pipelines with win probabilities, a board with drag and drop and a keyboard “Move to…” menu, and a stage-grouped list with a move sheet on phones.
  • Several contacts per deal with roles, line items from a product catalogue or WooCommerce, won and lost with reasons.
  • Weighted forecast, an attention panel and a pipeline report with CSV download.
  • One-step “new deal” with its contact and company. Deals on contact and company pages, and on Today.
  • Custom fields on deals; segments by deal; tasks and timelines on deals.

0.2.0

  • Custom fields for contacts and companies: text, number, date, choices, yes/no, links, email and phone.
  • Tags, lists with permanent unsubscribes, and editable lifecycle stages.
  • Advanced filters and saved segments, with a live count.
  • Contact timeline with notes, calls, meetings and emails, plus automatic history.
  • Tasks with due dates and priorities, and a Today screen with what is due.
  • CSV import with column matching, duplicate handling by email and a consent check for lists; CSV export with a guard against spreadsheet formulas.
  • Merge duplicate contacts; bulk actions on many contacts at once.
  • Each screen loads on its own, so the mobile app starts faster.

0.1.0

  • First release: contacts, companies, roles, activity log, settings, the wp-admin app and the installable mobile app, in English and Spanish (Mexico).

short_description: A complete CRM inside WordPress, with an app that installs on your phone.
description:
Stedica CRM keeps your contacts and companies inside your own WordPress site, in your own database, with no limit on records or users. There is no account to create, and the plugin contacts no other site unless you turn on something that needs one: External services below lists each.

Contacts and companies

  • Unlimited contacts, companies and users, custom fields of every common type, and tags, lists and lifecycle stages you can rename, reorder, add and remove.
  • Each email address belongs to one contact, and possible duplicates (same name or phone) can be merged, history and all, or marked as different people.
  • Data-quality checks flag invalid and throwaway emails, domains that take no mail, shared mailboxes, missing names and broken phone numbers.
  • Optional company logos from each company’s own website, and legal details from Companies House, GLEIF, SEC EDGAR and the French company directory.
  • If two people edit a record at once, nobody’s changes are lost.

Deals and pipelines

  • Unlimited pipelines with their own stages and win probabilities, on a drag-and-drop board or a list.
  • Several contacts per deal, line items, won and lost reasons, a weighted forecast, and deals that went quiet.

Quotes, invoices and the client portal

  • Turn a deal into a quote in one click, with taxes per line, discounts, terms and your logo. Clients get a print-ready page and accept by typing their name or decline with a reason.
  • An accepted quote becomes an invoice in one click. Numbers use your prefixes and never repeat; record payments by transfer, card, cash or check. With WooCommerce, clients can pay through your checkout.
  • A client portal block where contacts you invite see their quotes and invoices, download shared files, update their details and email choices, and request their data or its deletion.

Timeline, tasks and reports

  • A timeline of notes, calls, meetings, emails and changes for each contact and company, tasks with due dates and owners, and a Today screen.
  • Connect a shared mailbox over IMAP and emails from or to your contacts land on their timeline. Other mail is ignored, and the mailbox is never changed.
  • Reports on pipeline, team activity, lead sources, email, automations, store revenue, quotes and invoices, and data quality, each downloadable as CSV.

Segments, import and export

  • Filter contacts by any field, tag, list, task or company detail and save it as a segment that stays up to date. Tag, list, assign or delete in bulk.
  • Import a CSV with columns matched for you, or move from FluentCRM, Jetpack CRM, WP ERP, WP-CRM System, Groundhogg, MailPoet, FunnelKit Automations, HubSpot, Mailchimp or your site’s users. Consent is never invented.
  • Someone who unsubscribed from a list is never put back on it by an import, a bulk action or a merge.
  • Export any list or segment to CSV, with sensitive fields left out unless an administrator asks for them.

Lead scoring that explains itself

  • Fit (A to D) and Engagement (1 to 4) combine into a grade from A1 to D4. Fit rules are filters; engagement rules give capped points for visits, forms, email clicks, calls, meetings and deals, fading over a half-life you choose.
  • “Why this score?” lists every rule and point, and you can preview how many contacts a change would move. Templates for six kinds of business and a report on how each grade converts.
  • Contacts who object to profiling are not scored, and sensitive fields never feed a rule. Scores decide whom to follow up first, never decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

Email campaigns

  • Newsletters to lists and segments, now or later, written in the block editor with merge tags, a phone preview and a test send.
  • Only people who consented or subscribed receive them; anyone who unsubscribed, bounced or complained is left out, checked again before each email.
  • Unsubscribe links, one-click unsubscribe and your postal address in every campaign; subject A/B tests, per-link reports and a send log.
  • Send through WordPress’s own mail (any SMTP plugin works), Amazon SES, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, Brevo or Resend; Site Health checks your SPF, DMARC and DKIM.

Automations

  • Build a flow from a trigger and steps, or start from one of twelve recipes.
  • Triggers: contacts, deals, quotes, invoices, forms, emails, WooCommerce orders and carts, accounts, website visits, dates, segments, webhooks, or by hand.
  • Steps send emails, update the contact, create tasks, deals and notes, notify your team, send webhooks and start other automations, with waits, if/else branches and goals. Automation emails follow the campaign consent rules.

WooCommerce and Easy Digital Downloads

  • Every order adds or updates the buyer’s contact with their orders, lifetime value (less refunds) and RFM segment. Past orders import in the background, and paid orders can become won deals.
  • Abandoned carts are saved once a shopper types their email at checkout; shoppers in the EU, the UK and unknown countries tick a box first. Up to three optional recovery emails link back to the filled cart.
  • Block and classic checkouts, either order storage, and Easy Digital Downloads orders.

The plugins you already use

  • Courses from Tutor LMS, LifterLMS, LearnDash and Stedica LMS; memberships and subscriptions from MemberPress, Paid Memberships Pro, Kadence Memberships (Restrict Content Pro), WooCommerce Memberships and WooCommerce Subscriptions; bookings from LatePoint and Amelia; tickets from Fluent Support and SupportCandy; answers from Stedica Surveys.
  • Their events reach the contact’s timeline, automations and lead scoring. Each is off until you turn it on.

AI assistants and the command line

  • WordPress Abilities let AI assistants and MCP tools search contacts, log calls, add tasks, move deals and explain scores, with the signed-in user’s permissions. Each is off until you turn it on.
  • AI assist, off until you turn it on, summarises a contact, company or deal and drafts emails through the AI service connected to WordPress 7.0 or later. Email addresses, phone numbers and custom fields are never sent.
  • wp stedica-crm commands to import, export, recount, rescore, purge and send a test email.

Forms, consent and website activity

  • A form block or shortcode (inline, pop-up or slide-in) with spam filtering and no captcha, or your forms in WPForms, Gravity Forms, Fluent Forms, Contact Form 7, Formidable Forms, Ninja Forms, Elementor Pro or Stedica Surveys. List sign-ups confirm by email first.
  • A Restricted content block shows a lead magnet once the visitor sends a form that adds the right tag.
  • Every consent, withdrawal and objection is kept, never edited, with the exact wording shown.
  • Website activity, off until you turn it on: the pages a contact visited, their searches and where they first came from, with the consent rules in the FAQ.

Mobile app

  • Add your site’s /crm/ address to a phone’s home screen for a full-screen app made for one hand; the same app runs inside wp-admin.
  • An optional offline copy on each device; changes made offline are sent once back online.
  • Task reminders as notifications on phones and computers, once an administrator turns push reminders on.
  • A Manual button beside every page title, and a dashboard widget.

Roles, privacy and languages

  • Five roles: CRM Admin, CRM Manager, CRM Sales, CRM Marketing and CRM Viewer. Optionally, sales users see only their own and unassigned records, enforced on the server for every request.
  • An activity log, personal-data export and erasure, retention limits and suggested privacy-policy text. See the FAQ.
  • Each user sees the CRM in their own language. Translations come from translate.wordpress.org, where you can help translate Stedica CRM.

External services

The plugin uses an outside service only when you choose one: an email provider, a mailbox, an automation webhook, an import from HubSpot or Mailchimp, AI assist, push reminders, company logos, a company registry or a Premium licence.

Email. Until an administrator picks a provider in Stedica CRM → Settings → Email, all email goes through WordPress’s own wp_mail(). The chosen service is called only to send the plugin’s emails (campaigns, automation emails, team notices, tests, recovery and confirmation emails, quotes, invoices and one-to-one emails). Each email gives it the recipient’s and sender’s addresses and names, the reply-to address, subject, HTML and text body, unsubscribe headers and a send number, which it returns with bounce and complaint reports.

  • Amazon SES: email.<region>.amazonaws.com, plus Amazon SNS certificates from sns.<region>.amazonaws.com to verify bounce reports. AWS Customer Agreement, Privacy Notice.
  • Postmark: api.postmarkapp.com. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.
  • SendGrid: api.sendgrid.com. Terms of Service, Privacy Notice.
  • Mailgun: api.mailgun.net or api.eu.mailgun.net. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.
  • Brevo: api.brevo.com. Terms of Use, Privacy Policy.
  • Resend: api.resend.com. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.

Site Health’s SPF, DMARC and DKIM checks use your server’s own DNS lookups.

Mailboxes. Until an administrator connects one in Stedica CRM → Settings → Mailboxes, no mail is read. Then, every five minutes and on Check now or Test connection, the plugin signs in to the IMAP server entered, over SSL/TLS or STARTTLS, with its user name and password (stored encrypted), opens the chosen folders read-only and reads what arrived since the last check. It never marks, moves or deletes a message, and keeps only emails from or to your contacts. The server belongs to your mail provider (such as Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or your host), whose terms and privacy policy apply.

Automation webhooks. A “Send a webhook” step posts JSON to the https address entered in it, when a contact reaches the step: the contact’s ID, email, first and last name, phone, job title, lifecycle stage, grade, tags and lists; the automation’s ID, name and trigger; your site’s address; and a delivery number and time. The address belongs to a service you chose, whose terms and privacy policy apply.

Imports. Stedica CRM → Import contacts reads from HubSpot or Mailchimp only while someone previews or runs an import with a key they enter. The key is sent with each request and never saved. Nothing about your site’s contacts is sent: only the key, the fields to read, record ids and page markers, and your site’s address in the user agent.

  • HubSpot: api.hubapi.com, with a private app access token; reads contacts, companies and notes. Customer Terms of Service, Privacy Policy.
  • Mailchimp: <dc>.api.mailchimp.com, the data center at the end of the API key (such as us21); reads audiences, fields and members. Standard Terms of Use, Privacy Statement.

AI assist. Off until an administrator turns it on in Stedica CRM → Settings → Integrations. It uses the AI client built into WordPress 7.0 and later, so requests go to the AI provider connected to your site, under that provider’s terms and privacy policy. A request goes out only when a user clicks Summarise on a contact, company or deal, or Draft with AI in the email form. It contains the record’s name, job title, company, lifecycle stage, grade, tags, deal or order figures and up to 30 recent timeline entries (type, date and subject); a draft adds what the user typed and their name. Email addresses, phone numbers and custom fields are never sent.

Push reminders. Off until an administrator turns them on in Stedica CRM → Settings → General; then each person chooses per device. Their browser gives the plugin an address at its push service, kept only if it belongs to a service below. When a task falls due (or 15 or 60 minutes before), the plugin posts the task’s title, a short heading and a link to the app to that address, encrypted end to end so the push service cannot read it, with a signed token naming your site’s address. Test notifications work the same way.

  • Google (Chrome and other Chromium browsers): fcm.googleapis.com. Firebase Terms, Privacy Policy.
  • Mozilla (Firefox): *.push.services.mozilla.com. Terms of Service, Firefox Privacy Notice.
  • Apple (Safari and Home Screen apps on iPhone and iPad): web.push.apple.com and *.push.apple.com. Legal, Privacy Policy.
  • Microsoft (Edge): *.notify.windows.com. Services Agreement, Privacy Statement.

Company logos. Off until an administrator turns them on in Stedica CRM → Settings → Company data. The plugin asks each company’s own website for its home page and the icon it names, or /favicon.ico, every 30 days and when the website changes, sending only what WordPress sends with any request (including your site’s address in the user agent). The company’s own terms apply. Turning logos off deletes them.

Company registries. Used to look up a company’s legal name, registration number, status and registered address. Each is off until an administrator turns it on in Stedica CRM → Settings → Company data, and is called only when someone searches, picks a result or clicks Refresh on a company. The request carries what they typed or the number picked, and nothing about your contacts.

  • Companies House (UK company register, run by the UK government): searches and company details from api.company-information.service.gov.uk, sent with the administrator’s free API key (stored encrypted). Terms of use: GOV.UK terms and conditions and the API developer guidelines. Privacy policy: Companies House personal information charter.
  • GLEIF (Legal Entity Identifiers): searches and records from api.gleif.org. Terms of use: LEI Data Terms of Use. Privacy policy: GLEIF Privacy Policy.
  • SEC EDGAR (US public companies, run by the US Securities and Exchange Commission): the list of company names from www.sec.gov (kept for a day) and company details from data.sec.gov. The SEC asks automated clients to identify themselves, so requests carry your site’s name and admin email address in the user agent. Terms of use: Accessing EDGAR Data. Privacy policy: SEC Privacy Information.
  • Annuaire des entreprises (French company directory, SIRENE, run by the French government’s digital agency DINUM): searches and company details from recherche-entreprises.api.gouv.fr. Terms of use: API Recherche d’entreprises access conditions and data.gouv.fr terms of use. Privacy policy: Annuaire des entreprises privacy policy.

Mail-domain check. On by default (turn it off in Stedica CRM → Settings → Company data): your server’s own DNS resolver is asked whether each contact’s email domain has a mail server. Common free providers are skipped, answers are kept 30 days, and nothing is sent to the address.

Freemius, for the optional Stedica CRM Premium. The bundled Freemius SDK sends nothing unless an administrator opts in, starts the trial or activates a licence. Then api.freemius.com receives the site’s address, that user’s name and email, and the WordPress, PHP and plugin versions; no CRM data. An upgrade link opens Freemius’s checkout at checkout.freemius.com in the browser; the plugin itself sends nothing to it. Terms of Service, Privacy Policy. The SDK is GPL-3.0.
